stories.subtitle: Along a vanished shoreline, recover a family letter written by three generations

stories.end: Telok Ayer Chinese Methodist Church → Tanjong Pagar MRT

stories.short_description: The sea has moved away, but the address on the family letter remains. Follow eight buildings to recover the signatures of three generations.
stories.theme_label: Letters from the Shore · Architecture puzzle
stories.hook: Near Fuk Tak Chi, the player receives a digital family letter addressed only to ‘Telok Ayer, by the sea’ — yet there is no sea in sight. The AI detects handwriting from three different eras and flags the letter as an impossible forgery. All that remains at the end is half a sentence: ‘If you can still find this street…’ The player must follow real buildings in search of delivery clues and decide whether the letter should be deleted, or delivered at last.

story_acts.title: Act One: A Shore Without a Sea (Stops 1–3)
story_acts.text: Trace the writer through the old shoreline, the marks of a five-county clan network and a note in another language. At first the player believes this is one Chinese family's story, then discovers the letter also passed through a South Indian port community. Each stop unlocks another layer of a dated map, rather than placing people from different eras in the same historical scene.

story_acts.title: Act Two: Why Was It Never Sent? (Stops 4–6)
story_acts.text: A mutual-aid ledger, a seafarer's wish and a schoolgirl's new handwriting gradually come to light. The AI tries to stitch them into one person's life story, producing a seemingly impossible span of years. The player realises the change in handwriting is not forgery: the next generation has begun writing for themselves, and the letter kept being continued as life went on.

story_acts.title: Act Three: Who Kept the Last Page? (Stops 7–8)
story_acts.text: The player first untangles a false contradiction caused by confusing ‘when the institution was founded’ with ‘when the building was completed’, then follows a Chinese-roof clue to the Methodist church. The last page comes from a fictional refugee in 1942. It explains why the letter spans different eras, and reveals that its final recipient is anyone in the future willing to understand this street.

stories.ending: The player restores the letter written by three generations: the first recorded how they arrived, the second how they learned and settled, the third how they found help in hard times. You may collect your ending card under the theme ‘Arrival’, ‘Mutual Aid’ or ‘Settling’; your choice changes the point of view, not the historical facts. Finally, the real historical timeline, sources and the eight-stop route you completed are shown.
stories.fiction_note: The letter, characters, seals, ledgers, notes, time windows, AI verdicts and level codes are all fictional, created for this project. We do not claim that the real venues hold these objects or ever passed this letter between them. Only each stop's historical_fact and its sources are researched history; no real place of worship is portrayed as a secret society, a curse or a criminal group.
stories.why_here: The eight stops line one street along the old shoreline, where landing at the port, faith, clan mutual aid, education and refuge are genuinely connected. NHB's ‘Telok Ayer: Bayfront Worship’ already links six of these buildings, and URA confirms the area was once the shore and a landing place for migrants. Lesser-known sites make up most of the route, with Thian Hock Keng Temple as a more familiar anchor in the middle. The former Keng Teck Whay building, Thian Hock Keng and Chong Wen Ge stand side by side, yet each carries its own chapter: mutual aid, seafaring faith and education.

stops.name: Fuk Tak Chi Museum
stops.historical_fact: Founded in 1824 as a small shrine by Hakka and Cantonese migrants, it also served as a centre of community mutual aid; it became a museum in 1998.
stops.story_reveal: The ‘by the sea’ on the letter is not a wrong address but an old geographical memory of a shoreline that has moved. The player receives the first layer of the old map, plus five place names not yet explained.
stops.task: Confirm the museum's name. From a safe public spot, compare the street with the in-game old-shoreline diagram (with sources) and choose ‘The address hasn't vanished; the shoreline has moved’. The wording and visibility of the on-site historical marker must be checked in field testing.
stops.next_hint: The five places on the letter — Meixian, Xingning, Wuhua, Pingyuan and Jiaoling — point to a clan association serving Hakka people from five counties. Look along the street for the ‘Ying Fo Fui Kun’ signboard.
stops.reward_card: History card ‘A Shore Without a Sea’ + story fragment ‘The First Unsent Letter’
stops.access_note: The Chinatown Singapore directory lists daily 10:00–22:00, free entry; reconfirm actual evening entry with the operator before launch. The NHB historical marker address is 80 (048466), outside the museum; the museum itself is at 76 (048464). Do not mix them up. When closed, a street-view exterior level is provided.

stops.name: Ying Fo Fui Kun
stops.historical_fact: Founded in 1822 to serve Hakka migrants from five counties in Guangdong; the association still stands on its original Telok Ayer site.
stops.story_reveal: The five place names turn out to be a network of people from the same home counties. The fictional writer looked for family not just through a postal address but through community organisations — yet another note on the letter comes from outside China.
stops.task: Confirm the association by its real signboard, then drop the five place names from the first stop into the ‘Hometown network’ slot. The names are based on the association's official website; do not claim the five counties are necessarily carved on the façade.
stops.next_hint: A new note reads ‘Coromandel Coast’ and ‘honouring a saint, yet with no saint's grave’. Take the building-outline card and look along the street for the twin-towered façade of Nagore Dargah.
stops.reward_card: History card ‘How Five Counties Became a Network’ + story card ‘A Note in Another Language’
stops.access_note: The official website lists Mon–Fri 08:00–16:00, tel. 6533 6726. Office hours do not mean visitors may walk in at any time; contact them first for groups and indoor visits. The main storyline is completed from outside.

stops.name: Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre
stops.english_name: Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre
stops.historical_fact: A memorial shrine to a saint, built by South India's Chulia community; the saint's remains are not buried here. Since 2011 it has housed the Indian Muslim Heritage Centre.
stops.story_reveal: The player discovers that ties in the port crossed languages and places of origin. A fictional interpreter reads the note on the letter and hands over a mutual-aid ledger page bearing thirty-six signatures.
stops.task: From a public spot, match the twin-tower outline of the front, then use the official evidence provided to tell a ‘memorial building’ apart from a ‘saint's burial place’ — so the fact that there is no grave is not turned into a mysterious mechanism.
stops.next_hint: The thirty-six signatures belong to a private mutual-aid organisation founded in 1831. The next building has a new name, but its old identity is Keng Teck Whay; look for a building with an octagonal upper storey on a square base.
stops.reward_card: Fun Fact card ‘A Memorial, but No Saint's Grave’ + story fragment ‘Thirty-Six Signatures’
stops.access_note: The operator's page lists Mon–Fri 10:00–17:30, Sat 09:00–13:00, closed Sun, tel. 6227 5090; current ticket prices not verified. The same page mentions an October 2026 restoration fundraiser — this does not mean it is closed, nor that it is fully accessible during restoration. The main storyline uses the exterior; going inside is optional.

stops.name: Former Keng Teck Whay Building / Singapore Yu Huang Gong
stops.english_name: Former Keng Teck Whay Building / Singapore Yu Huang Gong
stops.historical_fact: Keng Teck Whay was founded in 1831 by 36 Peranakan Chinese merchants as a private mutual-aid society; the original building later became the Yu Huang Gong (Temple of the Heavenly Jade Emperor).
stops.story_reveal: The ledger records how a fictional person received support — not the code of a secret society. The player begins to suspect the AI has mistaken the year the society was founded for the age of the building.
stops.task: Observe the silhouette, then piece the square base and octagonal upper storey on your phone back into the building model. You only need to match the visible shapes — no need to walk around the building or count all eight sides from the street.
stops.next_hint: The seafarer's wish card you receive reads ‘First give thanks for a safe landing, then learn to write letters.’ Look along the street for Thian Hock Keng, where Mazu is worshipped and which is tied to the voyages of Hokkien migrants; then follow the trail of education.
stops.reward_card: History card ‘The Mutual Aid of Thirty-Six’ + Fun Fact card ‘Square and Octagon’
stops.access_note: The Chinatown Singapore directory lists daily 09:00–17:00, free; reconfirm with the venue before launch. It is an active place of worship: use only the public exterior and areas open to visitors. 1831 is the year the organisation was founded; do not label it as the construction year of the existing building.

stops.name: Thian Hock Keng Temple
stops.historical_fact: Where Hokkien migrants prayed to Mazu for safe voyages; the existing large temple was built in 1839–1842, and also hosted clan and educational activities.
stops.story_reveal: The letter's first writer only hoped to arrive safely. Sorting the wish cards, the player notices the tone changes on the next page: the writer no longer asks when to leave, but how to live here.
stops.task: Confirm the name of Thian Hock Keng, then place the evidence cards ‘Crossing the sea to arrive’ and ‘Learning here’ in the right chapters. Observing visible architectural details is optional; the main storyline does not require photographing deities or worshippers, or entering the inner halls.
stops.next_hint: The new handwriting on the letter asks, ‘When will I be able to finish a letter with my own hand?’ Look for Chong Wen Ge, a historic place of learning right next to the temple, with the word ‘wen’ (writing) in its name.
stops.reward_card: History card ‘From a Wish at Sea to a Life on Land’ + story fragment ‘A Change of Hand’
stops.access_note: The temple's official website currently lists daily 07:30–17:00, last entry 16:45; use these hours rather than the 17:30 in the Chinatown directory. The Chinatown directory lists free entry. Respect worship and on-site photography rules.

stops.name: Chong Wen Ge
stops.historical_fact: Built in 1849 on the initiative of Tan Kim Seng, with donations from the Hokkien, Hakka and Teochew communities; next door, Chong Hock Pavilion opened Chong Hock Girls' School in 1915.
stops.story_reveal: The fictional schoolgirl can finally write her own letters. The handwriting that ‘couldn't possibly belong to one person’ actually comes from the next generation; the player begins to split the letter into a timeline of three generations.
stops.task: Place Chong Wen Ge (1849) and Chong Hock Girls' School (1915) on separate event cards, distinguishing buildings, institutions and the opening of a school. On-site signs are only for confirming location; do not merge neighbouring buildings under one name.
stops.next_hint: A note kept by the schoolgirl mentions a neighbour from South India, who arranged to meet at ‘the prayer house that went from attap hut to brick walls’. The new evidence card gives two years, 1827 and 1855, pointing to Al-Abrar Mosque.
stops.reward_card: History card ‘Who Could Write Their Own Letters’ + story fragment ‘The Second Generation's Signature’
stops.access_note: The Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan's official list confirms the address at No. 168. Unified visitor hours and ticketing for the whole historic space have not been verified; do not treat café opening hours as full access to the heritage site. The core experience uses the exterior; confirm indoor access separately. Chong Wen Ge, Chong Hock Pavilion and Chong Hock Girls' School must be labelled separately.

stops.name: Al-Abrar Mosque
stops.historical_fact: Begun as an attap hut in 1827 and rebuilt as a permanent building in 1855, it served South India's Chulia community; its narrow façade carries two minaret-like elements.
stops.story_reveal: The AI flags 1827 and 1855 as a contradiction; the player realises they mark the beginning of the community's place of worship and the completion of the permanent building. Once corrected, the AI admits its earlier ‘forged archive’ verdict was premature.
stops.task: Put 1827 under ‘Founded’ and 1855 under ‘Permanent building completed’. Read any visible heritage plaque first; whether the plaque and years are legible must be checked in field testing. If they can't be read, use a digital evidence card with sources instead.
stops.next_hint: Correcting the type of date unlocks the last two lines: ‘Begun 1889, took shape 1925’ and ‘A Western body, a Chinese pavilion roof’. Look along the street for Telok Ayer Chinese Methodist Church, which fits both clues.
stops.reward_card: Fun Fact card ‘One Place, Two Beginnings’ + story card ‘The AI Takes It Back’
stops.access_note: MUIS confirms the current address and tel. 6220 6306, with no unified visitor hours listed. The main storyline is completed from the public road; do not block worshippers' paths, do not turn religious rites into game tasks, and ask on site before entering.

stops.name: Telok Ayer Chinese Methodist Church
stops.historical_fact: The congregation began in 1889 and the existing building was completed in 1925; a Chinese pavilion sits atop a Western-style building. During the Second World War it sheltered about 300 people.
stops.story_reveal: A fictional refugee wrote the last page in 1942 and left the letter to the future. At last, the signatures of three generations fall into place: what lives on is not one person's age, but memories of life kept and passed on by different hands.
stops.task: From a safe public spot, match the outline of the Chinese pavilion roof, then use 1889 and 1925 to confirm the two types of date. Finally, arrange the evidence from all eight stops into a three-generation story and choose your collection theme to complete the ending.
stops.next_hint: The main storyline ends here. Head to the nearest suitable public resting spot to sort your ending card, then start real walking directions to Tanjong Pagar MRT; the exact meeting point must be decided by an on-site survey.
stops.reward_card: History card ‘Shelter Inside a Building’ + ending card ‘The Letter Is Delivered at Last’
stops.access_note: Still an active church; general visitor access hours and heritage tours have not been verified. The final level can be completed by observing from the public road, without entering the sanctuary. Game NPC lines must not be presented as testimony from real refugees.

signature_puzzles.name: Five hometowns, one place to receive letters
signature_puzzles.play: Collect the five hometown names at Fuk Tak Chi, then walk to the candidate buildings along the street and use the real signboards together with digital records to confirm the association that could reach these migrants.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: Meixian, Xingning, Wuhua, Pingyuan and Jiaoling match the five-county Hakka community recorded on Ying Fo Fui Kun's official website, so the answer is Ying Fo Fui Kun; the puzzle does not rely on adding or subtracting house numbers.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: Both stops sit on the same historic street, and the short walk lets players feel how closely places of worship and clan associations stood together. Signboard visibility must be rechecked on site; do not assume the five counties are carved on the façade.

signature_puzzles.name: The Square-and-Octagon architecture puzzle
signature_puzzles.play: Observe the shape of the former Keng Teck Whay building, then select and combine a square lower storey and an octagonal upper storey in the 3D model on your phone. Restoring the correct outline unlocks the mutual-aid history card.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: The shapes match the square plan and octagonal upper storey described in NHB sources; no fictional secret rooms, working mechanisms or objects that must be found inside are added.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: The answer comes from a distinctive, documented feature of this building and could not work at just any landmark. The public-road view and any obstructions must be rechecked on site; players are not asked to observe the hidden back of the building.

signature_puzzles.name: Correct the AI's two timelines
signature_puzzles.play: At Al-Abrar, sort 1827 into ‘Founded’ and 1855 into ‘Permanent building completed’, then use 1889/1925 and the Chinese-roof clue to walk to the Methodist church and make the second judgement.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: An institution's origins and the completion of its present building can be decades apart. Both sets of dates are backed by the venues or official bodies; after the puzzle, the game explains the types of evidence rather than declaring that historical sources contradict each other.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: Players see two buildings shaped by continuity and rebuilding, and their judgement about dates decides the next stop directly. Whether the heritage plaques show the years must be rechecked on site; if they are obscured, a sourced digital evidence card is provided.

stories.title: The Last Edition
stories.subtitle: A typesetting apprentice from 1938 must find seven stories still worth telling in today's Kampong Gelam.
stories.end: Finish outside Istana Kampong Gelam / Malay Heritage Centre, with an easy return to Bugis MRT
stories.estimated_distance: About 1.5–2.2 km, including the main MRT links and the return trip
stories.estimated_duration: 110–150 minutes, plus extra time for indoor visits
stories.estimate_note: A planning estimate based on streets and official addresses, not walking directions or a field measurement. Doubling back from Malabar to the Heritage Centre at the end is a deliberate story ending and may be adjusted after the site survey.
stories.short_description: A typesetting apprentice from 1938 can't find his print shop. Help him fill in seven pages across today's neighbourhood.
stories.hook: On Bussorah Street, the player receives a newspaper with no text on it. Amin, a typesetting apprentice who says he is from 1938, suddenly appears on the screen: his neighbourhood paper isn't finished, yet his print shop has become a hotel and the school has a new use. He thinks the neighbourhood has lost its stories. The player must help him recover seven pages and decide what the front page should finally say.

story_acts.title: Act One: Familiar Street Names, a Past Out of Reach
story_acts.text: On the street where pilgrims once stayed, and in front of the Yellow Mansion, Amin first recognises the neighbourhood through old place names and the ways houses were used in different eras. The player discovers that appearances, names and uses can change — one photo of today is not enough to tell who once lived here.

story_acts.title: Act Two: How News Travels from One Person to the Next
story_acts.text: From an old Chinese school to an old print shop, and on to a religious school, the player links education, printing and readers. Amin finally finds his print shop, but needs the player to turn the collected material into readable pages in a 3D typesetting level.

story_acts.title: Act Three: A Newspaper Must Also Write What Hasn't Happened Yet
story_acts.text: At Malabar Mosque, opened in 1963, Amin realises the building didn't yet exist in 1938, the year he set out. The player must keep the different eras apart rather than forcing every place into the same day. The new paper records the old neighbourhood, and the people who joined it later.

story_acts.title: Finale: Who Belongs on the Front Page?
story_acts.text: Near the former palace, now the Malay Heritage Centre, the player chooses the front page: seafarers, scholars, merchants, or everyone who shaped the neighbourhood together. The evidence collected supports one version about migration, literacy and connection; the real history does not change with your choice.

stories.ending: You get a collectable ‘My Kampong Gelam Neighbourhood Paper’, with seven places, the headline you chose, a line about your own discovery and expandable fact sources. In two-player mode, each player contributes one cultural connection they hadn't noticed at first, combined into a shared front page.
stories.fiction_note: Amin, the time travel, the blank newspaper, the quest dialogue and the page codes are all fictional. 1938 is the fictional character's starting year and does not mean every building on the route existed then. Each history card states its own date; the 3D print room is an artistic reconstruction.
stories.why_here: The printing history, schools, pilgrimage services, merchants' homes and different Muslim communities here are well documented. The Sultan keeps the old print-shop building and Aliwal keeps the old Chinese school building; these real changes of use drive the time-travel story.

stops.task: Place the source records for the Javanese merchant, the Hadhramaut family and the Kerala community on the area map, then link each to the buildings you've visited. Belonging to one neighbourhood doesn't mean sharing the same migration story.

stops.reward_card: Culture card: one neighbourhood, many migration paths

The AI tidies up the wording but never changes the fact cards.

stories.hook: Beside the old opera stage, the player receives a damaged piece of film. Mariam, a fictional continuity clerk, has left a plea for help: “Someone has cut the closing credits. story_acts.title: Act One: A Stage Without an Audience
story_acts.text: Between the temple and the stage at Goh Chor, the player recovers the first sound of community life. Then, at the Sim Kwong Ho shophouses, they discover that the building's name, its developer and its designer are not the same credit; for the first time, someone who was left out has a real identity.

story_acts.title: Act Two: The Street Goes on Screen
story_acts.text: Lam Yeo connects news and coffee to the name ‘Nanyang’. The Kwan Yow Luen shophouses bring the woman developer back into the story and reveal how the real streetscape found its way into film. At the water kiosk, the player discovers a kind of exchange that kept street life going and never had a price at all.

story_acts.title: Act Three: The Impossible 1991
story_acts.text: The Burmese Buddhist Temple shot shows that the temple on its present site was completed in 1991, contradicting the starting assumption that ‘every shot predates 1967’. The player separates the dates of the original temple, its relocation and the new building, and realises the shots come from a fictional time camera — they can't be treated as evidence from a real old film.

story_acts.title: Act Four: The Seventh Name
story_acts.text: Arriving outside the old studio on Jalan Ampas, the player discovers that Mariam wasn't looking for a famous director's lost work, but for an unfinished set of closing credits for the street. The clues gathered at seven stops — building, making a living, mutual aid, migration and expression — together answer who made this street.

stories.ending: The player combines seven character credit cards and seven historical evidence cards into fictional closing credits planned to run about 90 seconds, choosing to edit them by date or by how people's lives connect. A collectable personal deck and a replay of the 3D editing suite are generated at the end. Fact notes always keep their sources; Mariam and the time camera are always marked as fiction. Both editing styles can express different understandings — no single emotional choice is the only correct ending.
stories.fiction_note: Mariam, the time camera, the plea for help, the missing credits, all character dialogue and fictional props are invented. There is no evidence that the seven places took part in a single event; we do not claim to have found a real lost film, nor attribute any case or crime to real historical figures. Numbers, subtitles and route prompts on the game screen are not real inscriptions on site. Public exteriors and historical facts underpin the story; artistic 3D reconstructions must not be taken as precise historical restorations.
stories.why_here: Balestier's sites are close together and have directly verifiable narrative links: Sim Cheng Neo developed two important rows of shophouses, and the Kwan Yow Luen shophouses appear in a P. Ramlee film, which leads naturally to the Jalan Ampas studio. A temple built by labourers, traditional trades, charitable water provision and the migration of the Burmese community fill in life on the same street across different eras. Rather than forcing Queenstown's new town and the Portsdown military housing together, this street suits a compact story prototype better; Queenstown Library is also currently closed for renovation.

stops.name: Goh Chor Tua Pek Kong Temple and Old Opera Stage
stops.english_name: Goh Chor Tua Pek Kong Temple
stops.historical_fact: Founded in 1847 by Hokkien labourers from the sugar-cane plantations; the permanent opera stage beside it was built by Tan Boo Liat in 1906.
stops.story_reveal: Only a stage is left in the damaged shot. When the sound is restored, the player hears fictional labourers and audience members talking, and realises the street's memory belongs first to the people who gathered here.
stops.task: From a public spot, observe how the temple relates to the free-standing stage, and pick out on screen the spaces where performing and watching took place. If the stage is hidden, complete the same task with a sourced historical diagram; players don't need to enter the temple, step onto the stage or wait for a performance.
stops.next_hint: On the back of the unlocked stage shot, a fictional subtitle appears: “1926 — the name on the corner isn't the whole credit.” The map then marks 292–312 Balestier Road, prompting you to look for Sim Kwong Ho.
stops.reward_card: Credit card 01: Labourers and audience | A public stage; evidence: two different years, 1847 and 1906
stops.access_note: Designed around what can be seen from the public street in daytime; current visitor hours have not been fully confirmed. Do not block paths during worship or performances; never require entry into a religious space to finish.

stops.name: Sim Kwong Ho Shophouses
stops.address: 292–312 Balestier Road, at the junction with Kim Keat Road, Singapore
stops.historical_fact: Sim Cheng Neo developed these shophouses in 1926; the building's name comes from the words Sim Kwong Ho on the corner façade.
stops.story_reveal: The player assumed the building's name was the architect's. The archive shows the developer, the designer and the name belong to different people — and the woman developer's name returns to the credits.
stops.task: Place three sourced archive cards — “Sim Kwong Ho”, “Sim Cheng Neo” and “Westerhout & Oman” — into the slots for building name, developer and designer. The name on site is only for finding your way; the answers are also given in the digital archive, so no one has to read small lettering high up.
stops.next_hint: The developer's credit card unlocks the next frame: a newspaper page turns into coffee packaging, leaving the subtitle ‘Nanyang’ and 328 Balestier Road, pointing to Lam Yeo.
stops.reward_card: Credit card 02: The builder | A woman developer; evidence: the difference between building name, developer and designer
stops.access_note: Only the street façade and public walkways are used; do not enter upstairs homes or the back of shops. The façade name, the view of the corner and safe standing spots need to be confirmed on site.

stops.name: Lam Yeo Coffee Powder Factory
stops.historical_fact: The founder was once an assistant editor at Nanyang Siang Pau (a Chinese daily). He sold coffee along the street in 1959 and opened a shop with his wife in 1960; Lam Yeo means ‘Nanyang’.
stops.story_reveal: The same ‘Nanyang’ moved from the world of news into the coffee trade. The player discovers that changing jobs didn't erase a person's past, and that beyond a name there is a life worth keeping.
stops.task: Put three timeline cards from the digital archive in order — the newspaper, selling beans from a van and opening the shop — then pick the keyword linking the shop's name to the old job: ‘Nanyang’. Smelling coffee, buying anything or getting an answer from staff is never a condition for finishing.
stops.next_hint: At the end of the coffee shot, a fictional street storyboard appears: “1928 — same developer, different designer.” The map gives 412–418 Balestier Road, inviting the player to find the second row of shophouses.
stops.reward_card: Credit card 03: The breadwinner | From news to coffee; evidence: started in 1959, shop opened in 1960
stops.access_note: The operator's website couldn't be read this round, so current full opening hours haven't been confirmed by the operator. When the shop is shut, the stop can still be completed using the address, shopfront and digital archive; do not assume the coffee-powder shop is a café where you can sit and drink.

stops.name: Kwan Yow Luen Shophouses
stops.address: 412–418 Balestier Road, with focus on the corner at No. 412, Singapore
stops.historical_fact: Developed by Sim Cheng Neo and designed by Kwan Yow Luen in 1928; this row of shophouses once appeared in a P. Ramlee film.
stops.story_reveal: The developer from the second stop reappears, but the designer is different. The shot lines up with the corner building, and the player realises a real street once went into the movies — they aren't looking for a set built out of nothing.
stops.task: From a safe spot, compare the corner, the rows of windows and the shapes of the doorway guardians, match the simplified façade on screen to the right building, then link the shared developer back to the second stop. If the view is blocked, a sourced diagram can be used instead; players don't need to cross the road for a panorama, and no single contested reading of the relief figures is set as the only answer.
stops.next_hint: A fictional bill appears in the restored street shot, with the amount left blank; the subtitle points to the corner of Boon Teck Road and Balestier Road: “Find a transaction that never needed paying.”
stops.reward_card: Credit card 04: Watchers in the streetscape | A multicultural façade; evidence: the same developer and a film streetscape
stops.access_note: Observe the public exterior only; do not enter commercial or residential interiors. How visible the guardian figures and ornaments really are hasn't been surveyed; the level must keep an archive fallback mode.

stops.name: Boon Teck Road Water Kiosk
stops.address: Junction of Boon Teck Road and Balestier Road; associated institution at 1A Boon Teck Road, Singapore
stops.historical_fact: The charitable associations involved merged in 1950 and for many years gave free water and herbal tea to passers-by; NHB records that a water kiosk survives at this junction.
stops.story_reveal: The fictional bill didn't lose its price — this was always care given free of charge. The credits the player is recovering begin to reach beyond buildings and trade, to include the mutual aid that kept community life going.
stops.task: Using the sourced story of the water service, connect the right one of three relationships — selling, giving or lending — to the labourers and passers-by. The kiosk is only for finding your place on site; whether the two urns are full that day or cups are provided doesn't affect finishing, and no one is asked to drink.
stops.next_hint: Once you choose ‘giving’, the shot of the water turns into a fictional migration trail ending at 14 Tai Gin Road, with an odd year beside it: 1991. The player follows the trail to the Burmese Buddhist Temple to check the dates.
stops.reward_card: Credit card 05: The water-giver | Care without a price; evidence: water provision and charitable service
stops.access_note: The kiosk's current appearance, any small change in position and whether water is being served still need checking on site. Do not touch, move or occupy the facility; the stop can be completed without entering the charitable association. If the facility isn't there, switch to junction geolocation plus an archive task.

stops.name: Burmese Buddhist Temple
stops.historical_fact: The original temple was set up on Kinta Road in 1878, and the temple on its present site was completed in 1991; the marble Buddha was already enshrined in the old temple in 1921.
stops.story_reveal: A 1991 building could never appear in an ordinary film finished before 1967. The player sees through the false assumption: the time camera crosses eras and records a community carrying on — it isn't an old reel to be read directly as a historical source.
stops.task: Match three sourced events — ‘original temple founded’, ‘Buddha enshrined in the old temple’ and ‘present temple completed’ — to 1878, 1921 and 1991, then decide which event overturns the assumption that ‘every shot predates 1967’. The exterior and digital archive are enough; entering the main hall is only a voluntary visit.
stops.next_hint: With the years in the right order, the shot reveals a fictional clapperboard: “Jalan Ampas, No. 8, 1967.” The edges of the seven cards begin to join into a reel of film, pointing to the finale outside the old Malay film studio.
stops.reward_card: Credit card 06: A migrant community | Buildings move, memory carries on; evidence: separating change of place from the dates of events
stops.access_note: At the time of checking, the temple website listed daily 07:00–18:00, which may change for festivals and events; tel. 6251 1717, admin@bbt.org.sg. Religious rites come first and going inside is not required to finish; if it is closed or a visit isn't appropriate, use the exterior from a public spot and the digital archive.

stops.name: Former Malay Film Productions Studio
stops.address: 8 Jalan Ampas, Singapore; public street outside the former studio
stops.historical_fact: The Jalan Ampas studio resumed production in 1947, bringing together Chinese producers, Indian directors and Malay actors; it closed in 1967.
stops.story_reveal: Mariam's full fictional message finally appears: what was cut wasn't a real crime, but the credits of ordinary people who took part in street life. Film itself depended on collaboration across communities and behind the scenes, and the seventh shot brings the previous six stops together.
stops.task: From a confirmed public standing spot, read about the studio, then first collect the seventh credit card and evidence card; next, link each of the seven character cards to its historical evidence and cut them into closing credits by date or by how lives connect. Arrival is confirmed by street name and address; if the house number is hidden, use the map and archive instead — you don't need to see anything inside the compound.
stops.next_hint: The slate card you receive gives the number of the final shot. Open ‘Finish the credits’ in your deck to close the case — there is no eighth stop to visit.
stops.reward_card: Finale collection card: The credits I wrote for this street; saves your personal cut for replay
stops.access_note: No current public access arrangements have been obtained. Only stops outside on the public street are planned; do not assume the studio interior can be visited, and never ask players to contact a caretaker, knock or pass the gate. Whether the pavement suits 2–4 people standing must be surveyed; if not, complete the finale at a nearby safe public spot.

signature_puzzles.name: Two credits
signature_puzzles.play: At the second stop, collect three archive cards — building name, developer, designer; at the fourth, rotate a simplified 3D façade and connect the two rows of shophouses, discovering the developer is the same but the designers differ.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: The answer is decided by the roles clearly recorded by URA, not by players guessing what names mean. Sim Kwong Ho is the building's name; both rows share the developer Sim Cheng Neo; the designers were Westerhout & Oman and Kwan Yow Luen respectively.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: Two real shophouse rows that can be linked on foot form evidence across stops; seeing the second building changes how you understand the card from the first stop. The façade on site is only a support — if it's blocked, the digital archive still works.

signature_puzzles.name: A cup of tea without a price
signature_puzzles.play: Stop five turns a commercial bill into a gift, then lays out water routes across an abstract 3D neighbourhood to supply several workplaces. The basic version takes three minutes; harder routes can be a post-game challenge.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: The historical answer is the charitable nature of the water service. Capacities, routes and water carriers in the game are fictional mechanics and make no claim to reconstruct historical transport records.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: The real water kiosk shows players that it wasn't only trade that kept the neighbourhood going. No drinking, buying or operating the facility is needed; if the site changes temporarily, junction location and sourced archives let you carry on.

signature_puzzles.name: The last seven shots
signature_puzzles.play: Stop six exposes the clash of dates; at stop seven, enter a fictional 3D editing suite, pair seven fact cards with credit cards, then choose a chronological or a thematic cut to create your own closing credits.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: Pairing facts with dates has a fixed basis; emotional expression and editing order allow many reasonable results. The 1991 completion of the present temple versus the studio's 1967 closure proves this material belongs to a fictional time camera, not a real old film.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: Players have been to seven real places, and the finish is a real former film studio, so editing isn't a stand-alone mini-game — it gathers the geographical and historical evidence from the walk into their own understanding.

Please find the seven names.” The time camera she left behind shows frame after frame on the street corners: shophouses, coffee packaging, a bill with no amount. At first you think it's just an old film reel — but the years that turn up next won't let that idea stand. Take the evidence, and find the time each shot belongs to.

preview_steps.full_ending: You put the last name back in the credits, and Mariam's film finally runs without a break. The labourers beside the stage, the builders of the shophouses, the people who gave water and the communities who moved here all reappear in the picture of the street. The temple completed in 1991 still belongs to its own era; the fictional time camera simply lets it meet shots from before 1967. As the screening ends, seven names remain on the screen. You remember these connected lives — and who it was you stopped for along the way.

constraints: field_verified is false for every stop; this file is a research and story plan, not a game that has been deployed or field-tested.
The main storyline relies on public outdoor spots and digital archives; venues being open, buying things, answers from staff or taking part in rites must never be required.

House numbers, façade details, markers, crossings and safe standing space at all seven stops must be confirmed on site; visitors must never be asked to stand in the road, in residential spaces or in closed courtyards to get a shot.

Lam Yeo's full current opening hours haven't been confirmed by the operator, so a closed-shop mode must be supported. The smell of coffee and working machines can add to the experience but must never be a required clue.
The Burmese Buddhist Temple website currently lists 07:00–18:00, which may change for special events and holidays; this only affects optional visits inside. Source: https://www.bbt.org.sg/contact/

Sun Yat Sen Nanyang Memorial Hall has been closed for restoration since 2024-09-16 until 2027; it is not a required stop and players are not asked to pass through its grounds. Source: https://www.sysnmh.org.sg/en/whats-on/events/closure-notice

Balestier Market has been re-tendered and is being repurposed, so the 24-hour food centre information on old pages is not guaranteed; it is not set as a required stop for food, toilets or going inside. Source: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/singapore-land-authority_slatenders-adaptivereuse-builtheritage-activity-7467769561665212416-vjTp

stories.title: The Missing Years: Finding the City's Lost 25
stories.subtitle: From the Gate of Hope to a virtual waterfront race, use clues from public life to repair a city's time
stories.area: Bras Basah / Civic District / Marina Bay
stories.start: CHIJMES Gate of Hope, Victoria Street side; reached from Bras Basah or City Hall station
stories.end: Tan Kim Seng Fountain, north end of Esplanade Park; walkable to Esplanade or City Hall station
stories.estimated_duration: About 2–2.5 hours, including walking, reading cards, puzzles and one round of a proposed virtual race
stories.estimate_note: An editorial estimate, not calculated by walking-route software or walked on site. Only publicly accessible ground-level areas are used; roads are crossed only at open junctions or pedestrian crossings. Race duration and the existing 3D game's performance have not been tested.
stories.short_description: The city has lost 25 years. Read the evidence of public life, then use three racing clues to find the last fountain.
stories.hook: You open FindSG, and the city clock suddenly rewrites the year on every history card to 2026. The only surviving hint: ‘You've missed 25 years.’ A fictional archive restorer asks you to recover the gifts, donations and ordinary lives the system has deleted. When you reach the waterfront, the clue is locked inside an on-screen race; finish it, and you'll learn which fountain to look for at the end.

story_acts.title: Act One: Not All Time Is on the Clock Face
story_acts.text: The Gate of Hope offers old records of children taken into care, and the Hill Street police station reveals that a government building was also home to police families. The system's error gradually shows itself: it keeps only buildings' names and looks, deleting the people who lived in the city and helped it. The bronze elephant leaves a card about a gift between nations, proving the same place can hold different eras and uses.

story_acts.title: Act Two: Recovering the City's Reference Points
story_acts.text: The surveying story at Cavenagh Bridge explains what a ‘benchmark’ is; the obelisk links merchants, trade and public works; the Victoria clock tower shows how public timekeeping and names leave traces of their era. After collecting three fictional calibration cards, players can start a round of the proposed race on the public waterfront promenade, chasing a time error inside the digital archive.

story_acts.title: Act Three: One Fast Lap, Then a Slow Read of 25 Years
story_acts.text: The race happens only on screen. Three fictional sectors give WATER, DONOR and FOUNTAIN in turn; these are in-game caption props and never real track signs. Players cross-check them with the Tan Kim Seng character card from the obelisk to unlock the next stop, Tan Kim Seng Fountain. On arrival, the 25 years between the 1857 donation and the 1882 memorial finally solve the riddle.

stories.ending: The player enters 25 and returns the two date cards — ‘donation’ and ‘memorial’ — to 1857 and 1882. The clock restores the city's many layers of time. The so-called stolen 25 years were a gap left because the fictional system only recorded when memorials were completed, missing the public contributions that came before. The player receives the digital collection card ‘City Timekeeper: Time Doesn't Belong Only to the Fastest’, and can open each real source to see what is fact and what is only game story.
stories.fiction_note: The archive restorer, every year turning into 2026, the calibration cards, the three English words in the race and the clock malfunction are all original fiction. Real people are never given private conversations or secret actions without evidence. Historical facts follow each stop's source_urls. The existing 3D game was not examined or integrated; we do not assume its track, years, assets, code, interfaces or completion callbacks are compatible with this plan.
stories.why_here: The route brings at least five rarely told historical details into one compact district: the Gate of Hope, the bronze elephant, the surveying benchmark story, the Dalhousie Obelisk and Tan Kim Seng Fountain. Their real common thread is public life in a port city: care, administration, international exchange, surveying, trade, timekeeping and water supply. The ‘city clock’ is an editorial narrative built on this material and does not claim that a secret organisation ever linked the eight points. For background on Bras Basah's schools, religion and intellectual life, see NLB: https://curiocity.nlb.gov.sg/digital-stories/bras-basah/bb-early/ .

stops.name: Gate of Hope
stops.address: Victoria Street side of CHIJMES, 30 Victoria Street, Singapore 187996
stops.historical_fact: From 1854 the convent cared for abandoned baby girls; this gate was named the Gate of Hope in 1996.
stops.story_reveal: The first thing erased isn't a building's date but the care that once happened behind the gate. The player receives a fictional archive page, ‘Ordinary People's Time’.
stops.task: From the public walkway on Victoria Street, confirm the gate and its sign and read a short history; if you can't find the sign, use the fact card directly. Don't open the gate or look into private spaces, and never treat the experience of abandoned babies as horror.
stops.next_hint: The next building has colourful windows, but its past was not only about law enforcement — it also held the everyday lives of police families. Follow legal crossings via Stamford Road/Hill Street to the Old Hill Street Police Station.
stops.reward_card: History card: Public care behind a gate; fictional calibration fragment A
stops.access_note: Use only the open street-side walkway and visible signs; CHIJMES Hall wedding venues and other indoor spaces are not required stops. Private events and site hoardings take priority.

stops.name: The family side of the Old Hill Street Police Station
stops.english_name: Former Hill Street Police Station — public exterior
stops.historical_fact: Completed in 1934, the building provided not only police facilities but also homes for officers and their families, along with a children's playground.
stops.story_reveal: The restorer realises the label ‘office building’ hides memories of home life; the city database has squeezed human lives into a building's function.
stops.task: From a public spot where you won't block anyone, look at the exterior and choose ‘Policing + family life’ rather than offices alone. This stop doesn't require entering government offices.
stops.next_hint: Walk along open public roads and the riverbank towards Old Parliament Lane; look for a king's gift that didn't come from Europe.
stops.reward_card: History card: A police station that was also home; fictional calibration fragment B
stops.access_note: Now used as government offices. Look at the exterior only, follow security and visitor rules, and don't enter office areas or treat any office entrance as a game zone.

stops.name: The Siamese bronze elephant at Old Parliament House
stops.english_name: Bronze Elephant Statue outside The Arts House
stops.address: Outside The Arts House, 1 Old Parliament Lane, Singapore 179429
stops.historical_fact: The bronze elephant commemorates King Rama V's visit in 1871. It was set up in front of the Town Hall in 1872 and moved in 1919 to where it stands today, in front of The Arts House.
stops.story_reveal: An object can change place and still keep its memory. The inscriptions on four sides of the elephant show players that the city's reference points were never in just one language.
stops.task: Observe the elephant from a spot where the public may stop, and solve the ‘Language of a Gift’ puzzle: use the official fact card to identify English, Siamese (Thai), Jawi and Chinese. You don't need to read every script, nor crawl around the plinth.
stops.next_hint: Walk south from The Arts House towards the river and stop at the north end of Cavenagh Bridge. The next clue isn't a treasure arrow, but a surveyor's shared point of reference.
stops.reward_card: History card: An 1871 diplomatic gift; fictional language calibration card
stops.access_note: Use only the open public paths outside The Arts House; do not enter the chamber or performance spaces. During ceremonies, events or hoardings, use the remote fact card instead.

stops.name: The surveying benchmark story at Cavenagh Bridge
stops.english_name: Cavenagh Bridge North Abutment — benchmark interpretation stop
stops.address: Public riverside path at the northern end of Cavenagh Bridge, near Asian Civilisations Museum, Empress Place, Singapore
stops.historical_fact: NHB records that the north abutment holds a survey benchmark from around 1882, marked with a broad arrow and a horizontal line to show a known reference height.
stops.story_reveal: The city clock has forced different eras into the same coordinate system; players must first restore the ‘reference’ before they can judge whether a year is really wrong.
stops.task: Pause on the public walkway at the bridgehead and identify the benchmark using a redrawn standard survey symbol and the NHB fact card. Looking for the original mark is only a skippable suggestion; never ask anyone to go under the bridge, down the riverbank, over railings or to lean out to look.
stops.next_hint: Walk along the public path on the north bank towards the Dalhousie Obelisk — a monument to a visit that holds evidence of how local merchants hoped to change the city.
stops.reward_card: History card: The survey benchmark; fictional calibration fragment C
stops.access_note: The location in the sources has been verified, but whether the original mark can be clearly seen from the public walkway in 2026 hasn't been checked on site. The location point is the safe bridgehead walkway, not the mark itself; finding the mark is never a condition for passing.

stops.name: Dalhousie Obelisk
stops.address: Empress Place, near Asian Civilisations Museum and Victoria Theatre & Concert Hall, Singapore
stops.historical_fact: The obelisk commemorates the Governor-General's visit in 1850; local merchants including Tan Kim Seng raised the funds, and used it to show their support for free trade.
stops.story_reveal: The player receives the character card ‘Tan Kim Seng: merchant and public benefactor’. The fountain's location isn't revealed yet — only the clue that he did more than business.
stops.task: Look at the monument's shape and public signage, and separate two different events: ‘the 1850 visit’ and ‘being moved later’. Players aren't asked to memorise disputed details of the move.
stops.next_hint: Walk north from the obelisk to the Victoria clock tower. The clock face tells the time now, but the old name left on the building tells of an earlier age.
stops.reward_card: Character card: Tan Kim Seng, who supported public water supply; the person and his contribution are kept, and the year the fountain was set up is revealed in the finale
stops.access_note: Stop on the public walkway to observe; don't climb the plinth, and don't make museum entry or gallery opening a condition for visiting the monument. When events restrict access, the on-site part may be skipped.

stops.name: The Victoria clock tower and an old name that never disappeared
stops.english_name: Victoria Theatre & Victoria Concert Hall — clock tower exterior
stops.historical_fact: The Memorial Hall was renamed Victoria Concert Hall in 1979, but its outer wall still bears the old name; the central clock tower links the two buildings.
stops.story_reveal: What the clock lacks isn't a clock, but the ability to let one place keep many eras at once. Three fictional calibration cards combine into permission to ‘Enter the simulator’.
stops.task: Observe the clock tower and the building's name only from outdoor public areas. Use the fact card to compare Memorial Hall and Concert Hall; players aren't asked to climb the tower, enter the auditorium or wait for the hourly chime.
stops.next_hint: Head for the open walkways near Queen Elizabeth Walk / Jubilee Bridge at the south end of Esplanade Park. Use pedestrian paths; the race entry point is on your phone, not on the Esplanade Drive carriageway.
stops.reward_card: History card: The city's public time; fictional simulator launch card
stops.access_note: Climbing the clock tower and indoor venue tours are separate activities that need booking and are not part of this free exterior route. Event closures on public roads, squares and building forecourts take priority.

stops.name: Waterfront public promenade · Clues of water and a donor
stops.english_name: Queen Elizabeth Walk / Jubilee Bridge vicinity — waterfront clue stop
stops.address: Candidate standing area on an open public pedestrian path at the southern end of Esplanade Park, near Queen Elizabeth Walk and Jubilee Bridge, Singapore; exact pin pending site check
stops.historical_fact: The 2026 Singapore Grand Prix runs from 9 to 11 October; the official Connaught grandstand information links Esplanade Bridge with Turn 14.
stops.story_reveal: The player has reached a waterfront area next to the real race circuit's city setting, but enters a fictional archive simulator. ‘Finishing a lap fastest’ isn't the ending — finding the public contribution that was left out is.
stops.task: At a currently open public pedestrian spot suitable for stopping, compare the Tan Kim Seng character card with the three fictional clues WATER / DONOR / FOUNTAIN to identify the next stop, Tan Kim Seng Fountain. Completing the three-word clue task is enough to continue; race results are not a prerequisite.
stops.next_hint: WATER + DONOR + FOUNTAIN, combined with the Tan Kim Seng character card: head north along the open walkways inside Esplanade Park to find Tan Kim Seng Fountain. Don't imitate the race along the roadway, and there's no need to cross the whole of Jubilee Bridge.

Jubilee is Gate 6 in the race guide and must not be treated as a free entrance during the race period. During the race, set-up, dismantling or other hoardings, the on-site trigger is closed and a remote unlock from a legal resting spot is provided; users without tickets are never guided towards the gates. Exact stopping areas and location tolerance must be confirmed on site; no precise coordinates are given for now.
stops.source_design_task: At a lawful, open public spot suitable for stopping, stand still or sit down to play a round of the proposed 3D phone race. Three fictional game sectors hand out three cards in turn: WATER, DONOR and FOUNTAIN. Combined with the Tan Kim Seng character card you already have, choose Tan Kim Seng Fountain from the bilingual list of candidate places to unlock Stop 8. Simply finishing the race is enough — there's no need to win. If the race won't load, the player chooses assist mode or can't finish, an equivalent matching task with the same three cards gives the same progress; if roads are closed on site, the alternative version is completed at a reachable legal resting spot, with online completion and on-site visits marked separately. This gameplay is still a design; interfaces for the existing racing project have not been obtained.

stops.name: Tan Kim Seng Fountain: the missing 25 years
stops.address: Esplanade Park, along Connaught Drive near Stamford Road, Singapore
stops.historical_fact: In 1857 Tan Kim Seng donated $13,000 to improve the public water supply; the fountain in his memory was set up in 1882.
stops.story_reveal: The system had only ever recorded the memorial's appearance in 1882, leaving out the public contribution of 1857. The 25-year difference is the answer to the mystery set up at the start.
stops.task: After confirming the fountain's name, read the two sourced fact cards in the app, put ‘donation’ under 1857 and ‘memorial’ under 1882, and work out the 25 years. Don't assume the plaque on site shows both dates; don't touch the basin, sculptures or railings.
stops.next_hint: Story complete. Return to the real map: you can take a nearby open pedestrian route to Esplanade or City Hall station, or simply take a rest.
stops.reward_card: Finale digital collectable: City Timekeeper; unlocks the full fact-and-fiction comparison page
stops.access_note: Esplanade Park is usually open 24 hours, but race and event closures still take priority. There are no physical prizes, staff or stickers to scan on monuments; if redemption is added in future, a place that clearly permits it must be chosen.

signature_puzzles.name: The Language of a Gift
signature_puzzles.play: Beside the bronze elephant, compare short samples of four scripts and find the one belonging to the giver; then return the 1871 visit, the 1872 statue and the 1919 move to separate event slots.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: The giver's script is Siamese/Thai. NHB records that the elephant's plinth carries English, Siamese, Jawi and Chinese — not simply today's four official languages. The events matched to each date all come from NHB.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: A seemingly ordinary sculpture keeps traces of international ties and of being moved; standing beside the object makes it easier than an abstract quiz to grasp that ‘a change of place doesn't mean history disappears’.

signature_puzzles.name: This arrow doesn't point to treasure
signature_puzzles.play: At the Cavenagh Bridge bridgehead, look at the broad arrow and horizontal line redrawn in the app and choose whether it marks direction, buried treasure or a height benchmark; following the official explanation, choose the line representing a known height.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: The answer is a shared reference for measuring elevation: the midpoint of the line marks the known height of that spot relative to the datum. The game doesn't require players to see the original mark, and certainly never directs them under the bridge.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: NHB records the physical benchmark from around 1882 on the bridge's north abutment and links it to the tidal surveys of the time; here the abstract idea of ‘calibration’ lands on real city infrastructure.

signature_puzzles.name: Three sectors, twenty-five years
signature_puzzles.play: View the concept render of the Stop 7 race and tap ‘Finish screen preview’ to collect three fictional clues — WATER, DONOR, FOUNTAIN — then choose Tan Kim Seng Fountain; the finale preview shows the 1857 and 1882 evidence and the answer, 25 years. The race doesn't run.
signature_puzzles.answer_logic: First deduce Tan Kim Seng Fountain, then work out 1882 − 1857 = 25. The English words on the track, sector rewards and completion events are game mechanics in design, not signs on real roads.
signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: Finishing the game produces a concrete clue to the next stop rather than just a badge; the race clock turns towards a contribution to public water supply, linking ‘speed’ and ‘time worth remembering’ into a story with an ending.

preview_steps.full_ending: You separate the 1857 donation from the 1882 memorial once more, and the clock stops at 25. The gap between two real dates is finally explained in this fictional archive repair. The fountain, the clock tower, the bridge and the gate each have their own time again, and the people who cared for others and supported public life return to the story. In front of the fountain you read the last evidence card, and the clock starts ticking again. This time, behind every number, there is room for people.

constraints: Checked on 2026-10-29; no field verification has been done, and field_verified is false throughout. Route distances, specific pedestrian links and safe stopping points need walking before launch; editorial estimates must not be treated as measurements.

The 2026 Grand Prix ran from 9 to 11 October; LTA announced road closures from 00:01 on 7 October to 05:30 on 13 October. That window has passed, but it can't simply be applied to the next edition, and roads reopening to vehicles doesn't mean every pedestrian area is free of hoardings. Source: https://www.lta.gov.sg/content/ltagov/en/newsroom/2026/9/news-releases/road-closure-and-transport-arrangements-f1-spore-grand-prix-26.html .

The Singapore GP requires everyone entering the Circuit Park to hold a valid ticket and use only the zones for their ticket type. Source: https://singaporegp.sg/en/faq/ticketing/purchases-and-orders/ . This route neither provides nor implies access to the track, paddock, grandstands or pit areas.

2026 Circuit Park map page: https://singaporegp.sg/en/event-info/circuit-park-map/ ; the official map file linked from the page: https://storage.singaporegp.sg/web/2026/circuit-park-map/circuit-park-map.jpg?1015= . Official Connaught information links the nearby Esplanade Bridge with Turn 14: https://singaporegp.sg/en/tickets/general-tickets/grandstands/connaught-grandstand/ . This is geographical background, not a metre-by-metre survey of the candidate trigger point.

Jubilee is Gate 6 in the GP's official exit guide: https://singaporegp.sg/en/event-info/eventguide/general/getting-here/getting-out/ . So during the race period, users without tickets must not be sent to that gate just because it's normally a public bridge.

On ordinary days, prefer open pedestrian areas near Queen Elizabeth Walk / Jubilee where people can stop; during the race and set-up/dismantling periods, the required geo-trigger here is switched off and players use an alternative unlock from a legal resting spot. Esplanade Drive and the Esplanade Bridge road sections of the track are never set as walking tasks.

The existing 3D game's URL, source code, assets, track version, mobile performance and completion events are all unknown; this file only defines the proposed product behaviour race_completed → unlock the fountain stop, and does not claim it has been integrated or verified. The full real track layout has not been calibrated corner by corner.

WATER / DONOR / FOUNTAIN in the race are clearly labelled fictional caption props; we don't claim the real F1 circuit has these signs, and players are never asked to run in real life or play while walking.

The public visibility of the original Cavenagh benchmark in 2026 hasn't been verified. The bridgehead story stop can be completed with the official fact card; going under the bridge, climbing railings or finding the tiny original mark must never be a required level.

NHB and venue sources differ on the year Tan Kim Seng Fountain was moved (1925 / 1929), so this story builds no puzzle on the year of the move; it uses the supported 1857 donation and 1882 memorial. Years for the clock tower's completion and the fitting of its clock are not used as answers either.

Although the Esplanade Park website lists it as usually open 24 hours, it also clearly prohibits commercial activity. This plan is designed for self-guided individual reading and walking; if it becomes a ticketed group activity, or adds set dressing, posted codes or fixed prize points, operating conditions must be checked again and permission can't be assumed. Source: https://www.nparks.gov.sg/visit/parks/park-detail/esplanade-park/ .
No racing, prizes or compulsory puzzles are built around the war memorial; the Lim Bo Seng Memorial game node has been removed from the final eight stops.

source_signature_puzzles.name: The Language of a Gift
source_signature_puzzles.play: Beside the bronze elephant, compare short samples of four scripts and find the one belonging to the giver; then return the 1871 visit, the 1872 statue and the 1919 move to separate event slots.
source_signature_puzzles.answer_logic: The giver's script is Siamese/Thai. NHB records that the elephant's plinth carries English, Siamese, Jawi and Chinese — not simply today's four official languages. The events matched to each date all come from NHB.
source_signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: A seemingly ordinary sculpture keeps traces of international ties and of being moved; standing beside the object makes it easier than an abstract quiz to grasp that ‘a change of place doesn't mean history disappears’.

source_signature_puzzles.name: This arrow doesn't point to treasure
source_signature_puzzles.play: At the Cavenagh Bridge bridgehead, look at the broad arrow and horizontal line redrawn in the app and choose whether it marks direction, buried treasure or a height benchmark; following the official explanation, choose the line representing a known height.
source_signature_puzzles.answer_logic: The answer is a shared reference for measuring elevation: the midpoint of the line marks the known height of that spot relative to the datum. The game doesn't require players to see the original mark, and certainly never directs them under the bridge.
source_signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: NHB records the physical benchmark from around 1882 on the bridge's north abutment and links it to the tidal surveys of the time; here the abstract idea of ‘calibration’ lands on real city infrastructure.

source_signature_puzzles.name: Three sectors, twenty-five years
source_signature_puzzles.play: The three fictional sectors of the on-screen race at Stop 7 give WATER, DONOR and FOUNTAIN; the player uses the Tan Kim Seng character card to deduce the next place. At the fountain, the finale is completed with the 1857 and 1882 fact cards.
source_signature_puzzles.answer_logic: First deduce Tan Kim Seng Fountain, then work out 1882 − 1857 = 25. The English words on the track, sector rewards and completion events are game mechanics in design, not signs on real roads.
source_signature_puzzles.why_location_matters: Finishing the game produces a concrete clue to the next stop rather than just a badge; the race clock turns towards a contribution to public water supply, linking ‘speed’ and ‘time worth remembering’ into a story with an ending.
